FLUIDS / SODIUM

Sodium

Uses the shared patient above. Choose high or low sodium, then plan the preparation and reassess the measured response.

Patient sodium & context

Measured patient Na and target fluid Na are separate values. Choose the workflow using the patient’s laboratory interval and clinical context.

HIGH sodium · Hypernatremia

Assessment checklist
  1. Assess perfusion, neurologic signs, hydration, and chronicity.
  2. Restore perfusion first if hypovolemic; investigate water access, water losses, renal concentrating ability, and sodium exposure.
  3. Plan controlled free-water replacement; tailor fluid sodium when needed and recheck the measured response.

LOW sodium · Hyponatremia

Assessment checklist
  1. Assess neurologic urgency and perfusion first.
  2. Confirm the result and glucose effect; assess volume status and chronicity.
  3. Investigate the cause, choose the fluid and initial correction plan, then recheck sodium.
For chronic hypernatremia, reference limits are 0.5 mEq/L/hr and 10–12 mEq/L/day. Free-water estimates do not replace perfusion resuscitation. AAHA reference.

2. Free-water replacement estimate

Blank duration uses 0.5 mEq/L/hr for chronic or 1 mEq/L/hr for confirmed acute context. The body-water fraction remains 0.6.

Free-water estimate

Assumes total body water = 0.6 × body weight in kg (liters). This starting-plan estimate does not predict serial measured sodium; account for other inputs and losses. Details & sources →

    Neurologic compromise or hypoperfusion: assess and stabilize urgently. The mixing cards are not a rescue-bolus protocol.
    Hyponatremia workup & investigation

    Urgent assessment

    Seizures or marked neurologic compromise require urgent evaluation for symptomatic hyponatremia; consider other causes concurrently. Stabilize hypoperfusion with a fluid selected to avoid an abrupt sodium shift.

    AAHA describes 2–6 mL/kg of 3–7.5% NaCl over 10–15 minutes for symptomatic cases, with reassessment. The mixing cards below are not this rescue-bolus protocol.

    Confirm & investigate

    • Repeat Na if unexpected; review assay/sample issues, glucose, and other chemistry findings.
    • Review GI/renal losses, third spacing, water intake, diuretics, desmopressin, and recent fluids; assess hydration and volume status.
    • Obtain urinalysis/USG and renal assessment as indicated. Consider measured osmolality and urine studies if the cause remains unclear.
    • In dogs with compatible findings, investigate hypoadrenocorticism; consider cardiac/hepatic/renal disease or inappropriate water retention according to the examination.
    Canine Addison’s testing reference

    AAHA: resting cortisol >2 µg/dL strongly excludes hypoadrenocorticism when assay-interfering glucocorticoids are absent. A lower result is not diagnostic; confirm with ACTH stimulation when indicated. Na:K ratio alone is not diagnostic.

    Sources and limitations

    Chronic/uncertain cases: use a conservative starting plan within 0.5 mEq/L/hr and 10–12 mEq/L/day; monitor the actual response. This is a focused ER workflow, not an exhaustive differential list.
